subject: ice-floats
title: Why Ice Floats: Water's Density Anomaly
summary: Directional hydrogen bonds make solid water about 9% bulkier than liquid, which shapes lakes, infrastructure and sea level.

keys.prompt: What is the molecular reason ice is less dense than liquid water?
keys.answer: Directional hydrogen bonds lock molecules into an open hexagonal lattice; in the liquid, broken bonds let molecules fill those cavities.

keys.prompt: Why does water reach maximum density near 4°C rather than at its freezing point?
keys.answer: Between 0 and 4°C, breaking hydrogen bonds lets molecules pack denser; above 4°C ordinary thermal expansion wins, so density peaks between.

keys.prompt: Why does melting floating sea ice matter far less for sea level than melting land ice sheets?
keys.answer: Floating sea ice already displaces water (Archimedes' principle); ice sheets on land add new water to the ocean when they melt.

cards.title: A liquid that reverses course
cards.text: Cool most liquids and they contract, then freeze into a denser solid. Water contracts too, until about 4°C. Then it reverses and expands, and it expands roughly 9% more as it freezes. That one anomaly decides whether lakes freeze solid, why pipes burst, and which melting ice actually raises the sea.

cards.question: It's February and a deep northern lake has a thick ice cover. What's the water temperature near the bottom?

options.text: Below 0°C, kept liquid by the pressure

cards.reveal: About 4°C. Water is densest near 4°C, so that water settles at the bottom, and in deep enough lakes the bottom stays near 4°C all year.

cards.title: Directional bonds, open lattice
cards.text: Water is strongly polar, and its hydrogen bonds are directional: each molecule bonds to neighbors at fixed angles. Freezing locks them into hexagonal ice Ih, an open lattice. At 0°C ice is about 0.9167 g/cm³ versus about 0.9998 for water, about 8.3% less dense, which is a 9% volume expansion. Hydrogen bonds are only about 5–10% as strong as covalent bonds, but they set this structure.
cards.example: Water isn't alone: silicon, gallium, germanium and bismuth also expand on freezing. But most substances shrink into a denser solid.

why.q: Why does a stronger, more ordered bonding network produce a less dense solid?
why.a: Because the bonds fix molecules at set angles, the ordered lattice is open, with cavities that the more disordered liquid can partly fill.

cards.title: Two effects, one peak at 4°C
cards.text: Two forces compete as water warms from 0°C. Melting breaks hydrogen bonds, and up to about 4°C that lets molecules fill lattice cavities, so density rises. Above 4°C, ordinary thermal expansion dominates and density falls. Near boiling, water is about 4% less dense than at 4°C.
cards.example: So 4°C water is the heaviest per liter, and in a cooling lake it's the water that sinks.

cards.title: Why lakes don't freeze solid
cards.text: Once surface water drops below 4°C, it's lighter than the water beneath, so the lake layers stably instead of mixing. Ice forms on top and insulates the rest. Even Lake Baikal in Siberia freezes only to about 1 m thick. If water were densest at freezing, cooling would keep overturning the lake until it froze from the bottom up.

why.q: Why would a lake whose water was densest at 0°C freeze from the bottom?
why.a: Cold surface water would keep sinking and mixing, so the whole lake would reach 0°C, and ice forming would collect from the bottom up.

cards.title: The 9% that costs money
cards.text: The same expansion is a force. Freezing water bursts pipes, a common cause of flooded houses. Freezing soil water heaves roads and building foundations. Repeated freezing in rock cracks drives freeze-thaw weathering. The trait that protects lake life is a steady expense for infrastructure.

examples_by_interest.business: Say you own rental homes in a cold climate. A vacant house with a furnace failure can turn freezing pipes into a flood, so heat and water shutoffs become part of the operating plan.

cards.title: Which melting ice raises the sea
cards.text: Archimedes' principle applies: floating sea ice already displaces water, so its melting isn't a major driver of sea-level rise. Ice sheets on land are different. Losses from the Greenland and Antarctic ice sheets add water to the ocean, and they're a major cause of sea-level rise.
cards.example: The kitchen version: a melting ice cube in a full glass doesn't overflow it, but adding ice from the freezer on top of the water would.

cards.question: Water's anomaly is a feature for lake ecosystems and a bug for infrastructure. Where else does one physical property cut both ways, and how do people design around it?
nudges: Think about thermal expansion in bridges, rails or concrete.
Is the cost of the bug borne by the same people who get the benefit?

questions.q: Which best explains why water is densest near 4°C?

options.text: Below 4°C, more hydrogen bonds hold an open structure; above it, thermal expansion dominates
options.why: Right. Two competing effects create a density peak between them.
Dissolved material changes density, but the 4°C peak is a property of pure water.

options.text: Water molecules get physically smaller at 4°C
options.why: The molecules don't change size. Their arrangement does.

options.text: Water molecules gain a little mass at 4°C
options.why: Mass doesn't change with temperature. Volume does, because the packing changes.

questions.q: A lake's surface is 1°C and its bottom is 4°C. What happens to the layers?

options.text: They stay put: the colder surface water is lighter
options.why: Yes. Below 4°C, colder water is less dense, so the layering is stable.

options.text: The surface water sinks because it's colder
options.why: That's the intuition from most liquids, but below 4°C colder water is lighter.

options.text: The lake mixes until it's 0°C throughout
options.why: That's what would happen if water were densest at 0°C.

options.text: The bottom water rises because it's warmer
options.why: Warmer here means denser, so the 4°C water stays down.

questions.q: Which ice melting would add the most to sea level?

options.why: Right. Land ice adds new water to the ocean when it melts.
Sea ice already displaces water, so it isn't a major driver of sea-level rise.

options.text: Floating ice cubes in a glass
options.why: The same Archimedes logic: they already displace their share.

options.text: Ice of either kind adds the same amount
options.why: Floating ice already displaces water; land ice doesn't.

sources.title: Properties of water
sources.supports: Water is strongly polar and forms hydrogen bonds, which give it a solid less dense than the liquid; density decreases about 9% on freezing; directional hydrogen bonds give ice and cold water open lattice structures; breaking bonds between 0 and 4°C allows denser packing as molecules fill lattice cavities, while above 4°C thermal expansion dominates; water near boiling is about 4% less dense than at 4°C; below 4°C lakes layer stably with floating ice insulating the water below; Lake Baikal freezes only to about 1 m; bottoms of deep enough lakes stay near 4°C year-round; if water were densest at freezing, lakes would mix and freeze bottom up; silicon, gallium, germanium and bismuth also expand on freezing.

sources.title: Ice
sources.supports: Ice is about 8.3% less dense than liquid water (a 9% volumetric expansion); ice density 0.9167–0.9168 g/cm³ at 0°C versus 0.9998–0.999863 g/cm³ for water; almost all ice on Earth is hexagonal ice Ih; expansion causes freeze-thaw weathering, frost-heave damage to foundations and roadways, and burst pipes that commonly flood houses; floating ice prevents bottom-up freezing; sea ice already displaces water due to Archimedes' principle, while losses from the Greenland and Antarctic ice sheets are a major cause of sea level rise.

sources.title: 10.1 Intermolecular Forces
sources.supports: Hydrogen bonding is a particularly strong dipole-dipole attraction between molecules with O-H, N-H or F-H groups, including water; hydrogen bonds are intermolecular and only about 5 to 10% as strong as covalent bonds, but strongly affect the properties of liquids and solids.
